BEL.story:
Most of Belgium's record concerns abuse of children by Catholic priests and members of religious orders, much of it in boarding schools after 1950. When Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges resigned in 2010 after admitting he had abused his nephew, a church-backed commission received 475 complaints in six months and counted 102 verified alleged abusers in about 29 orders. A parliamentary committee reported in 2011 that abuse had occurred in every sector of the church and across the country.

Time limits kept most of these cases out of court. An earlier church commission, from 2000, upheld 32 of 33 formal complaints, but 31 were time-barred and only one reached court. The legal deadline then ran 10 years after a victim turned 18. Church houses also sheltered an abuser wanted abroad. Fr Eric Dejaeger, a Belgian-born member of the Oblates (a Catholic missionary order), fled to Belgium in 1995 when he was about to be charged over Inuit children in Igloolik, Canada. Oblate officials knew he was leaving, and he lived in their homes for 16 years despite an international warrant until his return in 2011.

State institutions were part of the same pattern. Expert reports found abuse in Flemish youth institutions between 1930 and 1990, and the Flemish Parliament apologised in 2014. The Dutroux case exposed failures by police and courts. Marc Dutroux had been released early in 1992 from a 13.5-year sentence for rape; in 1995–96 he kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19, and rivalry between the Gendarmerie (the national police force of the time) and the judicial police slowed the search. He was convicted in 2004, and Belgium reorganised its police. Witness claims that he served an elite abuse network were dismissed by prosecutors and remain unproven.

Belgium also received adopted children with false papers. It took 3,697 children from South Korea between 1969 and 1995; a Korean truth commission found in 2025 that agencies there registered children with known parents as orphans. A Flemish review found that some children adopted from Ethiopia had not been given up voluntarily.

The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 27,862 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to Belgium in 2024, 235 per 100,000 people.

A compensation scheme for church victims has existed since 2012. A 2024 parliamentary inquiry found that prosecutors dismiss 58% of sexual-violence cases and asked for a study on ending the time limit for child sexual abuse retroactively.

BOL.story:
Bolivia's record covers abuse of minors in Jesuit schools over several decades and the sexual exploitation of children by foreign visitors and online buyers described by the US State Department.

Alfonso Pedrajas, a Spanish priest of the Jesuits (the Society of Jesus, a Catholic religious order), settled in Bolivia after his first abuse in Lima in 1964. In a diary published by the newspaper El País in 2023, he wrote that he abused at least 85 minors between 1972 and 2000, many at Jesuit schools. He confessed to a superior in 1978, who did not report it. Pedrajas died in 2009 and was never tried. In September 2025 a Bolivian court convicted two former heads of the Jesuit province, Marcos Recolons and Ramón Alaix, of knowing of the allegations and not reporting them, and sentenced each to one year; sentences under three years are normally commuted in Bolivia. Prosecutors said they would pursue other priests named at trial.

The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says foreign offenders exploit children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, around Rurrenabaque, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni. It says production of abuse material for sale online is rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz, and that Bolivian women and girls are sex-trafficked in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru. The Venezuelan criminal group Tren de Aragua is reported to be involved in trafficking in the country. NCMEC, the US centre that receives reports from online platforms, recorded 68,688 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to Bolivia in 2024, 553.3 per 100,000 people.

Bolivia is also home to closed German-speaking Mennonite farming colonies, about 150,000 people by a 2023 estimate; a mass-rape case in the Manitoba Colony led to convictions in 2011. The source does not say how many victims there were children.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scores criminal actors within the Bolivian state at 6.5 out of 10, and the US places Bolivia on its Tier 2 Watch List. Two Jesuit superiors have been convicted for not reporting abuse, while the abuser died untried. The scale of exploitation by foreign visitors and online buyers has not been measured.

CIV.story:
The record for Côte d'Ivoire comes mainly from the 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report and describes children moved within West Africa for work, where sexual exploitation follows. Distant relatives bring girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and neighbouring countries to Abidjan, promising school or training, and then keep them as unpaid domestic workers, where they are exposed to sexual abuse. Ivorian women and girls are sex-trafficked, especially in Abidjan.

Nigerian trafficking networks also bring women and girls into the country with offers of shop jobs and then exploit them in gold-mining and cocoa areas. The US report on Nigeria names Côte d'Ivoire among the mining destinations of these networks, some linked to Nigerian cult organisations or confraternities (closed secret societies).

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scores criminal actors within the state at 7 out of 10. Walk Free estimates 193,000 people in modern slavery in the country, all ages and forms. The US centre NCMEC recorded 66,461 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated there in 2024. Childlight, a research centre on child exploitation, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa have no representative survey data on online exploitation of children, so its true scale is not known.

DEU.story:
Most of Germany's documented cases come from studies of Catholic dioceses published since revelations at the Canisius-Kolleg school in January 2010. In Münster, historians found at least 610 minors abused by 196 clerics between 1945 and 2020, estimated the real number at 8 to 10 times higher, and found that bishops usually transferred accused priests. Fr Peter Hullermann, suspended in Essen over abuse of a boy, was accepted into Munich in 1980 under Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, given parish work, abused again, and kept serving until 2010; the Munich report found only 4 of 173 accused priests had been dismissed from the priesthood.

Public youth services placed children with abusers. From the late 1960s into the 2000s, Berlin youth authorities placed children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, in what is known as the Kentler experiment, after the sexologist Helmut Kentler. In Lügde, a youth office placed a foster girl with Andreas V., who with Mario S. was convicted in 2019 of abusing 32 children at a campsite; police had not acted on repeated complaints, and a state parliamentary inquiry said the men could have been stopped two years earlier. At the Odenwaldschule, a boarding school, victims came forward in 1998, but prosecutors dropped the case as time-barred.

Germany is a base for online abuse networks. German police shut down the dark-web forums Elysium, with over 87,000 members, in 2017 and Boystown, with 400,000 users, in 2021. Starting from one man in Bergisch Gladbach, police in 2019–22 traced a chat network with more than 30,000 pseudonyms and rescued 65 children. NCMEC, the US reporting centre, recorded 225,369 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to Germany in 2024, and the UK's Internet Watch Foundation acted against 18,401 web addresses hosted there in 2025.

German diplomats looked away from abuse abroad, as the federal president acknowledged in 2016. Paul Schäfer, wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, founded Colonia Dignidad in Chile in 1961; in 1966 the West German embassy said it found no evidence of abuse, and in 2006 a Chilean court convicted Schäfer of abusing 25 children. The colony's doctor, convicted in Chile in 2011 of aiding child sexual abuse, lives in Germany, where an investigation into him was dropped.

Since 2013 civil claims can be brought for 30 years, but the change did not revive claims already time-barred. Diocesan studies are still appearing; Paderborn's, in 2026, found abuse concealed there for decades.

ESP.story:
Spain's record covers the removal of children from their families under the Franco regime and afterwards, and abuse of children within the Catholic Church.

Under a 1940 law, imprisoned Republican mothers, women on the losing side of the civil war, could keep their children only until age three, after which the state took custody; 12,043 such children were in state custody in 1943. The regime, its welfare agency Auxilio Social and the Women's Protection Board, which confined women, removed about 30,000 children, and names were changed so that children could be given to pro-regime families. Babies of confined women were still being taken into the early 1980s. In 2008 Judge Baltasar Garzón described the removals as crimes against humanity. Prosecution has been held back by the 1977 Amnesty Law, by Women's Protection Board files that went missing in 1996, and by time limits; the first "stolen baby" trial, of Dr Eduardo Vela in 2018, ended without punishment because the time limit had passed.

The Ombudsman's 2023 report on the Catholic Church found its response to abuse often minimised or denied the problem. In a survey for that report, 0.6% of 8,000 adults said a priest had abused them as children; media applying the figure to the adult population reached about 200,000 victims of clergy. The bishops' own audit counted 2,056 minor victims. When the Marist Brothers recognised 25 victims in their schools in 2020, only one teacher had been tried because the other complaints were time-barred. The Catalan ombudsman found that religious orders had generally not searched for other victims.

Children in public care have also been exploited. On Mallorca, about 16 cases of sexual exploitation of minors in the care of the island's child-protection agency were known by January 2020; a 2021 commission found no network linking them, and two men were convicted in 2020 of corrupting girls in care.

Spanish offenders also appear abroad. Daniel Galván, a retired Spanish professor convicted in Morocco of raping 11 children, was pardoned by the Moroccan king in 2013 and left the country before the king revoked the pardon after protests; he was then imprisoned in Spain. Spanish National Police have led several online operations, one of which found many of the members exchanging abuse material in WhatsApp groups were themselves minors.

The bishops apologised in 2023 but disputed the media estimates, and the 1977 Amnesty Law continues to hinder investigation of the Franco-era removals.

GHA.story:
Ghana's record centres on children held in forced servitude, in shrines and on fishing boats, where girls are exposed to sexual abuse. Under trokosi, a practice among the Ewe people in Ghana and Togo, traditional shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing. The girls serve shrine priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders of the practice deny. Ghana made ritual servitude a crime in 1998, with a minimum sentence of three years, but the practice continued and the source records no prosecutions.

On Lake Volta, boat owners use trafficked children in fishing. A 2023 household survey of 1,286 children in three fishing districts by the charity International Justice Mission estimated that 37.7 per cent were likely trafficked and 45.1 per cent more were in likely exploitative child labour. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says traffickers use children as young as four, control them with violence and limited food, and that girls in fishing are vulnerable to sexual exploitation; it also notes reports that forced child labour on the lake has decreased.

Ghanaian children also appear in cross-border cases. Some of the more than 300 boys and men freed in 2019 from a building in Kaduna, Nigeria, presented as an Islamic school had been brought from Ghana; local media reported captives were tortured and sexually abused, and seven people were arrested.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scores criminal actors within the Ghanaian state at 7.5 out of 10. The US centre NCMEC recorded 51,598 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to Ghana in 2024, but Childlight, a research centre, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa have no representative survey data on online exploitation, so its scale is not known. Trokosi has been a crime since 1998, and the source records no prosecutions.

GUM.story:
Guam's record is the abuse of children within the Catholic Archdiocese of Agaña, the island's church, over several decades, and the legal reckoning that followed a change in the law. In 2016 Guam lifted the civil time limit for child sexual abuse claims, which allowed victims to sue for old abuse. More than 200 lawsuits followed, naming 35 clergy, teachers and scoutmasters.

The case at the top of the church concerned Archbishop Anthony Apuron. A Vatican tribunal of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, the church office that judges abuse by clergy, found him guilty in March 2018 of some charges including sexual abuse of minors, and rejected his appeal in February 2019. He was barred from office and from living in Guam but was not removed from the priesthood, and he denies the allegations.

Facing the lawsuits, the archdiocese filed for bankruptcy in January 2019. Claims rose to nearly 280; a January 2020 plan offered $21 million, and the archdiocese sold its Yona property for $6.1 million. Bankruptcy moved the claims out of open trials and into a single settlement process.

The US centre NCMEC recorded 404 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to Guam in 2024, 240.8 per 100,000 people. The church claims are being settled through bankruptcy; the record does not cover abuse outside church institutions.

IRL.story:
Most of Ireland's record is abuse of children in institutions that Catholic religious orders ran for the state, and in parishes. The Ryan Commission found in 2009 that more than 250 church-run institutions held over 30,000 children from the 1930s to the 1990s, that sexual abuse was "endemic" in boys' industrial schools run mainly by the Christian Brothers, and that state inspections failed. A 2024 state inquiry recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 orders.

Bishops dealt with complaints themselves. The Murphy Commission found in 2009 that four archbishops of Dublin failed to tell the Gardaí (the police) what they knew about abuse complained of by 320 people between 1975 and 2004, and that the archdiocese insured itself against claims from 1987, and that Gardaí treated priests as outside their remit. In Cloyne, nine complaints made between 1996 and 2009, after the church had adopted reporting rules, did not reach the Gardaí, and the inquiry said the Vatican's response to those rules allowed bishops to ignore them. Religious orders also moved offenders abroad. The Norbertine order moved Fr Brendan Smyth between parishes, dioceses and countries, including the United States; he was later convicted, and the BBC put his victims at 143 or more.

Mother and baby homes, run by religious orders, local authorities and the state, were part of an adoption system that hid children's origins. About 9,000 children died in these homes between 1922 and 1998, and several were linked to illegal adoptions, many to the United States. In 2018 the government found 126 people placed by the St Patrick's Guild adoption society had been falsely registered as their adoptive parents' children; a 2021 review estimated 5,540 to 19,980 adoption files might show similar signs.

In sport and scouting, a 1998 inquiry found a "total systems failure" in the swimming association, and Scouting Ireland accepted in 2020 that its predecessor bodies had shielded 275 known or suspected abusers.

Ireland was also the base of Freedom Hosting, a dark-web host for over 200 child abuse sites; its operator was arrested in Dublin in 2013 and convicted in the US. NCMEC, the US reporting centre, recorded 722 reports of suspected online child abuse per 100,000 people in Ireland in 2024.

A 2017 act lets Irish courts try Irish offenders for abuse committed anywhere. A redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000, but the Ryan report names no perpetrators, and the full extent of falsified adoption records has not been checked.

JOR.story:
The record for Jordan is thin and concerns Syrian refugee girls. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says Syrian refugee women and girls in Jordan have been sold into forced marriages, and that in 2022 Jordanian authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists. The same report describes how, in Türkiye, Syrian girls forced into unofficial religious marriages are then held in domestic servitude and sex trafficking; it does not say whether the same follows in Jordan.

Walk Free estimates 102,000 people in modern slavery in Jordan, all ages and forms, or 10 per 1,000 people. The US centre NCMEC recorded 37,728 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to Jordan in 2024, 326.6 per 100,000 people. Childlight, a research centre on child exploitation, found in 2026 that the Middle East and North Africa have no representative survey data on online exploitation of children. How many refugee girls have been sold into marriage is not counted in these sources.

LBN.story:
Lebanon's record concerns Syrian women and girls who fled the war and were then sold for sex inside Lebanon. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says criminal groups recruit them with false job offers and hold them in Lebanese brothels, and that Syrian children are held in bonded labour, work to pay off a debt, in the Beqaa valley.

The case on record shows how the trade survived police action. In March 2016 Lebanese security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels, Chez Maurice and Silver-B, in the Maameltein red-light district of Jounieh, and more than a dozen people were indicted on sex-trafficking charges. Human Rights Watch reported that Chez Maurice had been raided in late 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found trapped there, and had reopened after about three months. A survivor told the Lebanese publication Legal Agenda that a trafficker claimed he had "bought the state". The sources do not say how many of the women freed in 2016 were under 18.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scores criminal actors within the Lebanese state at 9.5 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.08 out of 10. The US centre NCMEC recorded 19,860 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to Lebanon in 2024. Childlight, a research centre, found in 2026 that the region has no representative survey data on online exploitation of children.

The 2016 raid is the main documented intervention. Recruitment of Syrian women and girls into Lebanese brothels continued to be reported in 2025.

MDG.story:
Madagascar's record is the commercial sexual exploitation of children, by Malagasy men and by foreign visitors. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says most child sex-trafficking victims are exploited by Malagasy men, and that foreign tourists, often from France, also exploit children. Parents sometimes encourage daughters into commercial sex with tourists, and children are exploited in karaoke bars in the capital, Antananarivo.

The country's place in this trade is tied to its region. Child sex tourism in Madagascar increased after Mozambique tightened its laws, with mostly French and Italian offenders. Another form is paid for by phone. In July 2025 police on the island of Nosy Be arrested two women suspected of filming abuse of their own children and selling the videos to foreign buyers through mobile money, and they were charged.

Courts convicted 15 traffickers in the US reporting year, the first convictions in four years. The US report calls corruption and official complicity significant concerns, and one official was investigated. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scores criminal actors within the state at 8 out of 10.

Foreign and local offenders continue to exploit children. The number of children affected is not counted in the sources.

MOZ.story:
Mozambique's record links the sexual exploitation of girls to war and its aftermath, and to the roads and mines where money and men gather. After the 1992 peace treaty, soldiers of the UN Operation in Mozambique (ONUMOZ), the UN peacekeeping force, recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. A 1996 UN study led by Graça Machel reported this and found that in 6 of 12 country studies the arrival of peacekeeping troops was associated with a rapid rise in child prostitution. Criminal responsibility for peacekeepers lies with the countries that send them, and the UN itself can only send them home.

The current conflict in Cabo Delgado province in the north has brought abduction by armed groups. The UN verified that armed groups, including the Islamic State affiliate known locally as Al-Shabaab, abducted 468 children there in 2024, 371 boys and 97 girls, 392 of them for recruitment, and committed sexual violence against 5 girls. In 2023 the UN attributed sexual violence against 12 girls to the Mozambique Defence Armed Forces (5), armed groups (4) and the police Rapid Intervention Unit (3), so state forces account for most of that year's verified cases.

Away from the conflict, the 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says traffickers exploit girls at rest stops, bars and restaurants along the highway from Maputo to South Africa and around mines. Girls as young as 11 who work as nannies are vulnerable when that work ends.

The country also hosted a church figure later sanctioned for abuse elsewhere. The Salesian bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo worked in Maputo from 2004; in 2020 the Vatican restricted his ministry and barred contact with minors over allegations that he had abused boys in Timor-Leste, but it did not disclose this until a magazine reported the case in 2022. The sources record no allegations against him in Mozambique.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scores criminal actors within the state at 9 out of 10. Abductions in Cabo Delgado continued into 2024, and exploitation along the highway and at mines is described but not counted.

NPL.story:
The largest part of Nepal's record is the movement of girls and women across the open border with India into brothels there. Nepal's National Human Rights Commission estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in 2018, 5,000 of them children, and that nearly 1,000 Nepali women and girls are rescued from India each year. Research collated on Wikipedia puts the number taken to India at 5,000 to 10,000 a year across a border of 1,850 km that has little screening. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says recruiters use job offers, marriage offers and online romance scams. Girls freed from brothels in the Indian city of Kolkata in 2015 carried fake adult identity papers, which the charity International Justice Mission said traffickers issue to underage girls.

The trade also runs inside Nepal. A 2024 study cited by the US found that most workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers in the US reporting year, and the US report records serious concerns of official complicity.

A second system gathers children into institutions. Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 10,905 children in 417 registered child care homes in 2021/22, and UNICEF estimates about 85% have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families, in areas such as Karnali, with promises of schooling, deliver the children to homes in Kathmandu and are paid commissions; researchers say the homes use the children to attract donations. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers the law requires. Nepal is also among the countries named in a 2023 commission report on SOS Children's Villages, a children's charity, which confirmed serious abuse allegations and cover-ups in several of its national branches.

These homes supplied intercountry adoption. Nepal sent 1,991 children abroad between 2003 and 2022. After a 2007 newspaper investigation described baby-buying and deception of birth families, Nepal halted all adoptions abroad. New rules followed in 2008, but a 2009 mission from the Hague Conference, the international body that oversees adoption treaties, found papers were still regularly falsified to make children adoptable, and that a USD 5,000 payment per child created incentives unrelated to the cost of care.

Trafficking to India and recruitment into care homes are both documented as continuing. Childlight, a research centre, found in 2026 that South Asia has no representative survey data on online exploitation of children.

PNG.story:
The only documented part of Papua New Guinea's record is its use as a place to send Catholic priests accused elsewhere. New Zealand's Royal Commission into Abuse in Care found in 2024 that the church there transferred abusers to other ministries, and recommended an investigation into priests sent to Papua New Guinea after abuse allegations. It did not say how many were sent or what they did there.

The US places Papua New Guinea on Tier 3, its lowest rating for government action against trafficking. Walk Free estimates 93,000 people in modern slavery there, 10.3 per 1,000. No cases of child abuse inside the country are on this map.

ROU.story:
Romania's record begins in its state institutions for children. Decree 770 of 1966 banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were left in state orphanages and institutions for disabled children, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation. Abuse was reported to be common at the children's psychiatric hospital in Siret.

After Ceaușescu's government fell in 1989, television showed about 100,000 children in these orphanages, and the institutions became a source of children for adoption abroad. Private agencies charged €7,500 to €25,000 per child, and the German broadcaster DW reported that the system "quickly became awash in corruption". The US alone issued 5,285 visas to children adopted from Romania between 1994 and 2008. Romania halted adoptions and outlawed baby selling in 1991, imposed another moratorium in 2001 after a government commission found middlemen and officials had taken adoption funds, and still recorded 458 adoptions abroad in 2002. A June 2004 law, passed under pressure from the European Union, banned foreign adoption except by grandparents; by 2006 there were none.

The institutions still expose children to trafficking. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says children in government-run homes, especially girls in homes for people with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking, and that alleged complicity and negligence by government employees in such cases remained a concern. Roma children as young as 11 are "sold" into marriage.

Most identified victims are women and girls sold for sex in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK. Many are recruited by the "loverboy" method, in which a recruiter poses as a boyfriend. A group dismantled by Romanian and UK investigators in 2020, with 21 arrests, had exploited girls in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18 and then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. A group charged in Galați in 2021 used the same method and earned about €350,000. In the 1990s and early 2000s girls from Romania were among those trafficked into post-war Bosnia and Kosovo, where international soldiers, police and contractors were among the buyers; the sources record no prosecutions of them.

The UK's Internet Watch Foundation acted against 21,188 web addresses hosted there in 2025, 7% of its total, and 14% of the abuse material confirmed by the hotline network INHOPE was hosted in Romania.

Foreign adoption has been closed since 2004. Courts convicted 161 traffickers in 2024, while the recruitment of girls for sale in Western Europe and the risks to girls in state homes continue to be reported.

SOM.story:
In Somalia, sexual violence against children is tied to the armed conflict, and both armed groups and forces sent to protect civilians are documented as perpetrators. The UN verified the abduction of 887 children in 2024, 850 of them by Al-Shabaab, the Islamist armed group, mainly to recruit them. It verified sexual violence against 267 children, 265 of them girls. Al-Shabaab was responsible for 120 of these cases and unidentified perpetrators for 110. Government security forces were responsible for 14, 11 of them by the Somali National Army, and the Ethiopian Liyu Police, a regional force from Ethiopia, for 7. The UN Secretary-General noted a fivefold increase in gang rapes.

Foreign troops have also abused girls. Human Rights Watch documented in 2014 that soldiers of the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), mainly Ugandan troops at and around its headquarters and Burundian troops at their Mogadishu base, raped and sexually exploited women and girls. Four rapes and one sexual assault involved girls under 18, the youngest a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier in 2013. Many victims came to the bases seeking medicine or aid; interpreters gave soldiers access to them, and some women and girls were compelled into sex in exchange for money, food or medicine.

In the cases on record, children were reached through abduction by armed groups and through their need for aid. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) rates Somalia's resilience to organised crime at 1.88 out of 10, and the US treats it as a special case it does not rank.

Abductions and sexual violence by Al-Shabaab and by government forces were still being verified by the UN in 2024. The sources do not record prosecutions for the AMISOM cases.

TCD.story:
Chad's record covers an attempt by a foreign charity to remove children from the country, and sexual violence against girls by armed forces, including Chad's own army, at home and abroad.

In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in the eastern town of Abéché as they tried to fly 103 children to host families in France. The charity said the children were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region; Chadian authorities found most were from Chad and were not orphans. A Chadian court convicted six French members of attempted kidnapping in December 2007 and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour. They were transferred to France, and President Idriss Déby pardoned them in March 2008. Chad is recorded on this map as a country whose sending of children abroad for adoption was later closed or suspended.

The army is named in UN records. The UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province in 2022, and attributed 4 of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan to the same army. In the Lake Chad basin, where Boko Haram and the Islamic State's West African branch (ISWAP) operate, the UN verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa. Chadian soldiers serving with MISCA, an African-led force in the Central African Republic, were also among the troops accused by boys aged about 8 to 13 at the M'Poko camp in Bangui of abusing them in 2013–14, often in exchange for food or money; a UN-appointed panel in 2015 called the UN's handling of these accusations a "gross institutional failure".

The US rates Chad Tier 3, its lowest, and the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scores criminal actors within the state at 8.5 out of 10. Childlight, a research centre, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa have no representative survey data on online exploitation of children. The Zoé's Ark members were pardoned, and the sources record no prosecutions of Chadian soldiers.

TWN.story:
Taiwan's record is about children sent abroad for adoption. It sent 4,289 children overseas between 2003 and 2022, by Selman's count of intercountry adoptions, and remains open as a sending country. The sources do not document abuse or falsified papers in these adoptions.

A Taiwanese woman also appears in a cross-border case. In 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, from two Bangkok houses run by a company called Baby 101, which took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking.

The US rates Taiwan Tier 1. The US centre NCMEC recorded 42,648 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to Taiwan in 2024, 179.1 per 100,000 people. No case of abuse inside Taiwan is on this map.

VIR.story:
The record for the U.S. Virgin Islands concerns Jeffrey Epstein, the financier who owned the private island of Little St. James there, and the banks that kept him as a client. The territory's government and victims sued over a sex-trafficking operation they said was run partly from the island, with girls, some as young as 14, brought from the US mainland. Epstein died in 2019; his associate Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted in 2021. A 2009 civil complaint alleged, "upon information and belief", that Epstein also brought minor girls from Turkey, the Czech Republic and other countries; prosecutors in Ankara opened an inquiry in 2025 and have reported no findings.

The territory's lawsuits targeted the money around the abuse. The government reached a $105 million settlement with Epstein's estate and $62.5 million with the billionaire Leon Black. In December 2022 it sued JPMorgan Chase, claiming the bank ignored warning signs and helped Epstein; in 2023 JPMorgan agreed to pay the territory $75 million and to pay $290 million to nearly 200 victims in a separate class action. New York's financial regulator fined Deutsche Bank $150 million in 2020 for ignoring warning signs on Epstein, and UK regulators banned the former JPMorgan banker Jes Staley for misleading them about his relationship with Epstein.

These are civil settlements and regulatory penalties, with no criminal findings against the banks. The US centre NCMEC recorded 222 reports of suspected online child abuse geolocated to the territory in 2024. The sources do not document abuse in the islands outside the Epstein case.
